blocks.text: The Jacobian is the matrix of all partial derivatives of a function that takes in several inputs and produces several outputs at once, rather than just a single number. It directly generalizes the gradient, covered in the previous lesson, to functions whose output is itself a whole vector instead of a single scalar value.

blocks.alt: Several inputs feed a vector-valued function producing several outputs; every partial derivative of every output with respect to every input is arranged into the Jacobian matrix
blocks.caption: The Jacobian collects every partial derivative between multiple outputs and multiple inputs into one matrix.

blocks.text: This lesson stays at an introductory level, focused on building the matrix correctly for small examples and understanding why it matters for backpropagation through vector-valued layers, with only a brief, high-level mention of its role in normalizing flows.
1. From Scalar Output to Vector Output

Every function covered so far in this module, aside from a brief mention here and there, has produced a single number as its output, even when it took several numbers in as input. The gradient lesson covered exactly this case, several inputs, one scalar output, collected into a single vector of partial derivatives.

Many functions of real interest instead produce several numbers as output at once, a neural network layer that outputs a vector, a coordinate transformation that maps one point to another, or a probability distribution over several categories. The Jacobian is what is needed to describe the sensitivity of every one of those outputs to every one of the inputs simultaneously.
1.1 A Concrete Example of a Vector-Valued Function

Consider a function taking in two numbers, x and y, and producing two outputs, u equals x squared plus y, and v equals x times y. This is a genuinely vector-valued function, two inputs go in, two outputs come out, and it is exactly the kind of function the Jacobian is built for.
2. What the Jacobian Is: A Matrix of All Partial Derivatives

For a function with several outputs and several inputs, the Jacobian is the matrix formed by placing the partial derivative of each output with respect to each input into its own dedicated cell. Every row corresponds to one output, every column corresponds to one input.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
u = x**2 + y
v = x * y
J = sp.Matrix([u, v]).jacobian([x, y])
print(J)   # Matrix([[2*x, 1], [y, x]])

blocks.text: Each entry of this matrix is a plain partial derivative, computed exactly as covered in the partial derivatives lesson earlier in this module, holding every variable except the one being differentiated fixed. The only new step here is deciding where each of those partial derivatives belongs inside the matrix, based on which output and which input it connects.

It helps to picture the Jacobian as a small table with a clear address system, the row tells you which output you are looking at, the column tells you which input, and the cell itself tells you exactly how sensitive that output is to that input, holding every other input fixed.
3. Notation for the Jacobian

The Jacobian of a vector-valued function f is usually written as a capital J, sometimes with a subscript naming f, J subscript f. Some texts instead write it using the same partial derivative notation from earlier in this module, wrapped inside a matrix, the partial of the output vector with respect to the input vector.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Notation","Meaning"],"rows":[["J or J subscript f","the full Jacobian matrix of the function f"],["J entry i, j","the partial derivative of the i-th output with respect to the j-th input"],["partial u over partial x","a single entry of the Jacobian, matching row u, column x"]]}

blocks.text: 4. How the Jacobian Generalizes the Gradient

The gradient, covered in the previous lesson, is exactly the special case of the Jacobian where the function produces only a single scalar output rather than several. In that case, the Jacobian collapses down to just one row, and that single row is precisely the gradient vector.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
f = x**2 + y**2   # a single scalar output
J = sp.Matrix([f]).jacobian([x, y])
print(J)   # Matrix([[2*x, 2*y]]), a 1-row Jacobian, exactly the gradient as a row vector

blocks.text: 4.1 A One Row Matrix Is Still a Matrix

It is a useful habit to think of the gradient as a Jacobian with only one row, rather than as a fundamentally different object, since it makes the jump to genuinely multi-output functions in this lesson feel like a small, natural extension rather than an entirely new idea.
5. Building the Jacobian Row by Row

A reliable way to build a Jacobian by hand is one row at a time, treating each output as its own separate scalar function and computing its full gradient with respect to every input, exactly as covered in the gradient lesson, then stacking each of those gradients as one row of the final matrix.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
u = x**2 + y
v = x * y
row_u = [sp.diff(u, x), sp.diff(u, y)]
row_v = [sp.diff(v, x), sp.diff(v, y)]
J = sp.Matrix([row_u, row_v])
print(J)   # Matrix([[2*x, 1], [y, x]])

blocks.text: This row-by-row construction is exactly why understanding the gradient thoroughly before this lesson pays off directly, every row of a Jacobian is nothing more than the gradient of one of the outputs, computed and placed in its correct spot.
6. A Worked Small Example Computing a 2x2 Jacobian
Using the same function from earlier, u equals x squared plus y and v equals x times y, compute the full Jacobian and evaluate it at the point x equals 2, y equals 3.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
u = x**2 + y
v = x * y
J = sp.Matrix([u, v]).jacobian([x, y])
J_at_point = J.subs({x: 2, y: 3})
print(J_at_point)   # Matrix([[4, 1], [3, 2]])

blocks.content: {"headers":["Cell","Expression","Value at (2, 3)"],"rows":[["Row u, column x","2x","4"],["Row u, column y","1","1"],["Row v, column x","y","3"],["Row v, column y","x","2"]]}

blocks.text: Each entry answers a genuinely specific question, the entry in row v, column x, value 3, says that at this point, nudging x alone increases the output v at a rate of 3, holding y completely fixed, exactly the partial derivative interpretation carried over unchanged from earlier in this module.
7. Reading the Jacobian: Rows and Columns

It is worth committing the row and column convention firmly to memory, since mixing it up produces a completely wrong, transposed matrix. Every row belongs to exactly one output, every column belongs to exactly one input, and the entry where they meet is the sensitivity of that output to that input alone.

items: Reading across one row shows how a single output responds to every input, one at a time.
Reading down one column shows how every output responds to a single input, one at a time.
The diagonal entries, when the matrix is square, describe each output responding to the input that shares its position.

blocks.text: A quick sanity check worth running on any hand-built Jacobian is counting its rows and columns against the number of outputs and inputs the function actually has, a mismatch there almost always means an entry was placed in the wrong row or column during construction.
8. The Jacobian in Backpropagation Through Vector-Valued Layers

A neural network layer almost always takes in a vector of activations and produces a vector of outputs, exactly the vector-in, vector-out shape the Jacobian is built for. Backpropagating a sensitivity signal through such a layer, covered at the level of scalars in the chain rule lesson earlier in this module, requires multiplying by that layer's full Jacobian matrix rather than by a single scalar derivative.

Concretely, if an incoming gradient signal describes how sensitive the loss is to this layer's output vector, multiplying that signal by the layer's Jacobian, transposed appropriately, produces the corresponding sensitivity to this layer's input vector, exactly the quantity needed to continue backpropagation one layer further back.

code.content:
# Conceptual sketch: propagating a gradient signal backward through one vector-valued layer
# incoming_grad: sensitivity of the loss to this layer's output vector
# J: this layer's Jacobian, output entries as rows, input entries as columns
# outgoing_grad = J.T @ incoming_grad  (sensitivity to this layer's input vector)

blocks.text: 8.1 One Jacobian Per Layer, Every Backward Pass

Modern automatic differentiation frameworks compute exactly this kind of Jacobian-vector product internally for every vector-valued operation in a network, without ever forming the entire Jacobian matrix explicitly when it can be avoided, a practical shortcut covered further later in this lesson.
9. The Jacobian Determinant, Briefly

For a Jacobian that happens to be a square matrix, as many outputs as inputs, its determinant is a single number describing how much a small region near a given point gets stretched or shrunk in volume by the function, and whether that transformation flips orientation.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
u = x**2 + y
v = x * y
J = sp.Matrix([u, v]).jacobian([x, y])
print(J.det())   # 2*x**2 - y

blocks.text: A determinant near zero signals that the function is squashing a whole region of input space down into a much smaller region of output space near that point, effectively losing information locally, while a large determinant signals strong local expansion.
10. Change of Variables and Normalizing Flows

This determinant idea has a specific, important application in a class of generative models called normalizing flows. These models transform a simple probability distribution into a complicated one using a chain of invertible functions, and correctly tracking how probability density changes under each transformation requires exactly the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant of that transformation.

This lesson only introduces the idea at a conceptual level, the exact formula and its full derivation belong in a dedicated generative modeling lesson elsewhere on this platform, but it is worth knowing that the Jacobian determinant covered in the previous section is precisely the mathematical object that makes normalizing flows work correctly.
11. Why the Full Jacobian Is Rarely Formed Explicitly in Practice

For a layer mapping a vector of size one thousand to another vector of size one thousand, its full Jacobian would have one million entries, and real networks often have layers far larger than that. Explicitly constructing and storing a matrix that size for every layer, at every training step, would be prohibitively expensive.

blocks.title: Jacobian-vector products instead of the full matrix
blocks.content: In practice, automatic differentiation frameworks compute the effect of multiplying a Jacobian by a specific vector directly, without ever materializing the full matrix in memory, exactly the Jacobian-vector product sketched earlier in this lesson. This is dramatically cheaper than forming and storing the entire Jacobian explicitly.

blocks.text: This is a recurring theme that will resurface again in the Hessian lesson later in this module, the mathematical object itself, whether Jacobian or Hessian, is easy to define on paper for small examples, but forming it explicitly at the scale of a real neural network is often avoided entirely in favor of cheaper, indirect computations.

This same tradeoff, an easy-to-define object that is expensive to construct explicitly at scale, shows up again with the Hessian in the very next lesson, where the matrix in question describes second-order behavior rather than first-order sensitivity.
12. Common Properties of the Jacobian

items: It has one row per output and one column per input, never the other way around.
It reduces exactly to the gradient, as a single row, when the function has only one scalar output.
Its determinant, when the matrix is square, describes local volume scaling and orientation.
It is the object multiplied against a gradient signal when backpropagating through a vector-valued layer.
It is rarely formed explicitly at scale, since Jacobian-vector products are far cheaper to compute directly.

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example
Given the vector-valued function with outputs u equals x plus 2y and v equals 3x minus y, compute the full Jacobian and evaluate it at x equals 1, y equals 1.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
u = x + 2*y
v = 3*x - y
J = sp.Matrix([u, v]).jacobian([x, y])
print(J)                          # Matrix([[1, 2], [3, -1]])
print(J.subs({x: 1, y: 1}))       # unchanged, this Jacobian has no x or y dependence at all
print(J.det())                    # -1 - 6 = -7

blocks.content: {"headers":["Cell","Expression","Value"],"rows":[["Row u, column x","1","1"],["Row u, column y","2","2"],["Row v, column x","3","3"],["Row v, column y","-1","-1"]]}

blocks.text: Since both u and v here are purely linear combinations of x and y, this Jacobian happens to be exactly constant everywhere, the same at every single point, unlike the earlier worked example where the Jacobian entries genuinely varied with the point being evaluated.
14. Practice
Before checking the answer, compute the Jacobian of the vector-valued function with outputs u equals x squared minus y squared and v equals 2xy, then evaluate it at x equals 1, y equals 2.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
u = x**2 - y**2
v = 2*x*y
J = sp.Matrix([u, v]).jacobian([x, y])
print(J.subs({x: 1, y: 2}))

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: The Jacobian is Matrix([[2x, -2y], [2y, 2x]]). At (1, 2), this becomes Matrix([[2, -4], [4, 2]]). Notice this particular pair of functions is exactly the real and imaginary parts of squaring a complex number, a classic example where the Jacobian determinant, here 4 minus negative 16, equal to 20, describes how squaring stretches area in the complex plane.

blocks.text: 14.1 A Second Exercise: Recognizing the Gradient as a Special Case
Using the single scalar function f of x and y equals x squared y, write down its Jacobian as a matrix, and confirm it matches the gradient of f computed the way the previous lesson would compute it.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: The Jacobian of a single scalar output has exactly one row, Matrix([[2*x*y, x**2]]), and this row is precisely the gradient vector of f, (2xy, x squared), confirming the gradient is simply the one-row special case of the Jacobian covered throughout this lesson.

blocks.text: 15. Common Mistakes

items: Transposing rows and columns, placing inputs along the rows and outputs along the columns instead of the correct convention.
Forgetting that the gradient is just a one-row Jacobian, and treating the two as unrelated objects.
Assuming every Jacobian has a determinant, that only applies when the matrix is square, equal numbers of inputs and outputs.
Trying to form a full Jacobian explicitly for a large layer instead of relying on a Jacobian-vector product, which is what real frameworks do.
Confusing the Jacobian determinant with the Jacobian matrix itself, the determinant is a single number, the Jacobian is the whole matrix.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes disappear once the row-per-output, column-per-input convention from earlier in this lesson is treated as fixed and non-negotiable, checked explicitly before filling in a single entry of the matrix.
Key Takeaway

The Jacobian is the matrix of every partial derivative between a function's several outputs and its several inputs, one row per output, one column per input, and it directly generalizes the gradient, which is exactly the special case of a single scalar output collapsed down to one row. Its determinant, when square, describes local volume scaling, a fact used at an introductory level in normalizing flow models.

In practice, the Jacobian matters most for backpropagating sensitivity signals through vector-valued neural network layers, and real systems almost always compute cheap Jacobian-vector products rather than ever forming the full matrix explicitly, since a full Jacobian at real network scale would be far too large to construct directly.
